newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Toll rises as rescuers search earthquake rubble.
newsitem.headline: Toll rises as rescuers search earthquake rubble.

text.p: Rescue teams in eastern Venezuela on Thursday searched for children and office workers trapped under buildings toppled by a powerful quake that rocked the Caribbean coast, killing at least 46 people.
"Up to now we have counted 46 dead and 280 injured in the entire state," Sucre State Civil Defence Director Francisco Espin told reporters. He did not specify where the deaths or injuries occurred.

Schools and office buildings were flattened by the tremor -- measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale -- crushing children in their classrooms and workers in their offices. Authorities said the toll could rise.
Victims ranged from infants to the elderly. Another 500 families were left homeless by the South American nation's worst earthquake for three decades.
More than 18 hours later, survivors were being pulled from rubble.

Worst hit was the small agricultural town Cariaco about 295 miles (470 km) east of Caracas, where scores of homes and buildings were flattened, including two schools, killing at least 26, mostly children.
"The problem is very serious. The high school building fell to the ground and there were many children in classes," State Governor Ramon Martinez told reporters.
Dozens of distraught family members milled in the street facing the Raimundo Martinez Centeno high school, staring blankly as rescue workers searched.
Textbooks and furniture lay scattered. Several limbs could be seen in the wreckage.
"There is one classroom totally covered over with possibly 25 to 35 more children inside," one rescue worker said.
Tomas Pantoja, an arts teacher, said Wednesday was the last day of classes before the summer break for many pupils. About 500 pupils were inside when the quake struck, he said.
"The building collapsed as if it had been hit by a bomb," Pantoja said.
Jhonny Delgado, a fourth grade student, said he escaped through a hole in the rubble after sitting out the first tremor that lasted about 10 seconds.
In the historic state capital Cumana 40 miles (60 km) west, rescue efforts were concentrated on a six-story office building that fell like a pack of cards.
Authorities said at least eight bodies were pulled from the ruins but 11 people had been rescued.
"We don't know how many people are still in there but we know there are a lot because the quake hit during office hours," Jose Azocar, Cumana's fire chief, told reporters.
Firemen and medics swarmed over the rubble, removing debris and trying to keep contact with those buried.
Around dawn on Thursday a group clustered near one of the holes opened in the wreckage burst into cheers and applause. Shortly afterwards a woman was carried away on a stretcher.
Some survivors, trapped in the basement, kept in contact with the outside world by cellular telephones, Martinez said.
Up to 70 people were thought to have been in the building at the time of the quake.
Martinez declared the worst hit eastern Sucre state in emergency and called for urgent assistance from the government to provide lifting equipment and medical aid.
About 65 Red Cross and rescue workers left Caracas on an Air Force Hercules C130 late Wednesday with more than 14 tonnes of medical supplies and equipment.

The quake, the worst to hit Venezuela since 1967, struck about 3:25 p.m. EDT (1925 GMT) Wednesday, sending panicked people into the streets in cities and towns from the capital to the furthest eastern tip of the country.
The FUNVISIS seismological institute said the first quake measured 6.9 on the open-ended Richter scale.

The epicentre was about 30 miles (49 km) off Venezuela's northeastern Caribbean coast and there were 15 aftershocks, the last in the early hours of Thursday, they said. FUNVISIS warned that further aftershocks could occur.

The disaster overwhelmed the town of Cariaco, where about 13,000 live. Diego Carbonel hospital, which has just 30 beds, no X-ray machines or blood bank, treated hundreds of injuries, director Ramon Ward said.
But state-owned oil company Petroleos de Venezuela said production and export continued to flow smoothly. Venezuela is the largest exporter of crude oil to the United States.

Founded in 1521, Cumana is the oldest inhabited city in South America. However, most of its colonial architecture was destroyed in a massive earthquake in 1797. Wednesday's earthquake was the second major tremor to strike the city of 250,000 people this century, the last in 1929.
The 1967 quake, the last to cause serious damage in Venezuela, killed 215 in the capital and surrounding area, FUNVISIS officials said.
